findings.title: Device limit check is racy (count then insert)
findings.body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts the devices and then inserts in separate, non-atomic steps. Concurrent requests from new devices can all see count < limit and all insert, so the limit can be exceeded. The check also costs an extra COUNT query on every tag attempt that is not served from the local cache.

findings.title: Device tagging moved from async to synchronous in the auth path
findings.body: TagDevice used to run in a goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout and panic recovery. It now runs inline on the request context, so every anonymous request that is not cached waits on DB writes. A DB failure or panic is no longer isolated. Cancelling the request context can also abort the tagging.

findings.title: Cache is set before the DB write, so a rejected device is cached as tagged
findings.body: tagDeviceUI calls localCache.SetDefault(key) before CreateOrUpdateDevice. If the write fails (limit reached, or a transient DB error), the key stays cached for 29 minutes. During that time later requests from the device return nil and are let through as anonymous. This bypasses the limit. The first request is rejected, but the retry succeeds without ever being recorded.

findings.title: Zero rows affected is reported as a limit error
findings.body: updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached whenever no row was updated. That includes a device that exists but whose updated_at is outside the window. The error is correct only in the sense that the device is new and the limit is hit. Expired devices are rejected too, and any case that matches no row is reported as a limit error.

findings.title: Duplicate 30-day expiration constants
findings.body: The 30-day expiration is now defined three times: thirtyDays in impl.go, anonymousDeviceExpiration in anonstore, and anonymousDeviceExpiration in api.go. They can drift apart, and the limit window in the store could then differ from the usage stats and the list API.
